There are sixteen consonants: /b/, /k/, /d/, /g/, /h/, /l/, /m/, /n/, /ŋ/, /p/, /r/, /s/, /t/, /w/, /y/ and glottal stop /'/.[1] There are six vowels: /a/, /ɔ/, /e/, /i/, /o/, /u/. Stress does not appear to be phonemic. It occurs on word final syllables. /ina/ (iná)[2] 'mother' /ina na/ (iná na) 'mother mine' ... [sec. 4.2 Interpretation, typescript p. 8:] Long vowels have been interpreted as two short vowels [handwritten above: 'geminate clusters']. new_statements.quote: Umirey Dumagat has two classes of phonemes. There are sixteen consonants: /b/, /k/, /d/, /g/, /h/, /l/, /m/, /n/, /ŋ/, /p/, /r/, /s/, /t/, /w/, /y/ and glottal stop /'/. There are six vowels: /a/, /ɔ/, /e/, /i/, /o/, /u/. Stress does not appear to be phonemic. It occurs on word final syllables. /ina/ (iná) 'mother' /ina na/ (ina na) 'mother mine' [fn. 2: Marked for stress. Also note that all examples in this paper are written phonetically (indicated by brackets) only when they differ from the phonemic writing.]

Also note that all examples in this paper are written phonetically (indicated by brackets) only when they differ from the phone…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the final syllable of the word (illustrated with iná 'mother'; the enclitic phrase /ina na/ is given as a second hand-accented example).
new_statements.exceptions: None in MacLeod 1963 (hedged: 'does not appear to be phonemic'). Caveat from the later Antonio 2007 MA thesis: it treats accent and vowel length as distinctive vowel features and transcribes many roots with penultimate accent plus length ([tó:tul] 'walk', [bé:yed] 'pay', [mé:nit], [qéyen] 'no') beside final-accented roots ([regút], [gumatáŋ], [dumatóŋ]), and states that accent shifts to the ultima under -in/-an suffixation and retracts to the penult with maka-; so a Tagalog-type contrast may exist that MacLeod's preliminary analysis did not register.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('word final syllables') from isolated citation forms; the accent placement in the phrase example /ina na/ is hand-drawn and ambiguous in the scan. Preliminary phonemic statement based on 1961-62 fieldwork at Matawe, Dingalan, Quezon.
new_statements.identity_note: MacLeod 1963 describes the 'Umirey Dumagat dialect' as spoken at sitio Matawe, c. 8 km south of Dingalan, Quezon (Umiray River area = geographic centre; endonyms 'tagi keelogen'/'source Umirey' and 'tagibulus'), i.e. core Umiray Dumaget [umir1236], not the Anglat/Palaui Island varieties Glottolog lists as dialects. Antonio 2007 describes the same language under the name Tagebulos (Reid 1994: 'In Bulacan, the people refer to themselves as Tagabulos').

sources.note: Ch.2 (generative, SPE-style): 'aksent' (2.3.21) and 'lengt' (2.3.20) are listed among the distinctive features of vowels; no statement of where word accent falls. Sec. 2.5.2.3: with verb suffixes -in/-an 'May paglipat ng aksent sa ultima' (accent shifts to the ultima), e.g. /witik+-qan/ > [witikán]; 2.5.2.7 with maka- accent retracts to the penult ([maká:mit]). Transcriptions show both final ([regút], [gumatáŋ], [dumatóŋ]) and penult-with-length ([tó:tul], [bé:yed], [mé:nit], [qéyen]) accent on roots, i.e. data inconsistent with purely fixed final stress.
